analysis.one_liner: Bans new offshore oil and gas drilling off Florida's coasts.
analysis.headline: The bill to ban offshore drilling off Florida died in committee in the 116th Congress and never received a House vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred the Interior Department from offering any new oil and gas leases off Florida's coast, including the eastern Gulf of Mexico within 125 miles of the shoreline, the South Atlantic waters south of 30°43' North, and the Straits of Florida. It would not have affected leases issued before enactment. The goal was to protect Florida's beaches, fishing, and tourism economy from drilling and spill risk. It never advanced beyond committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Florida coastal residents, beachgoers, recreational and commercial fishers, and the tourism economy built on clean beaches and marine life. Military installations that use the Gulf ranges also gain from fewer drilling conflicts.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits new offshore oil and gas leasing and preleasing in the eastern Gulf of Mexico, the South Atlantic waters south of 30°43' N, and the Straits of Florida.
Protects Florida beaches, tourism, and fishing economies from the risk of oil spills associated with offshore drilling.
Preserves existing rights under leases issued before enactment, so the ban applies to future leasing only.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies would lose access to potential new offshore drilling acreage off Florida; consumers could see marginally higher energy supply costs if significant reserves go undeveloped.

drawbacks.text: Restricts domestic offshore energy development, potentially reducing future oil and gas supply and keeping some reserves off the market.
Only limits new leasing; existing leases remain unaffected, so near-term drilling risk is not eliminated.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit—reducing spill risk to Florida's heavily tourism- and fishing-dependent coast—is concrete and well-documented; the cost—less potential offshore energy development—falls on a single industry and is speculative in the near term. The tradeoff is modest and largely regional.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in January 2019 and referred to the House Natural Resources Committee, then to its Energy and Mineral Resources subcommittee; no further action was taken before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced on January 8, 2019 by Rep. Kathy Castor with bipartisan cosponsors including Reps. Rooney, Crist, and Buchanan.
Referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources on January 8, 2019.
Referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources on February 5, 2019.
No further action, markup, or floor vote occurred before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Offshore oil and gas interests benefit from the bill's failure, as potential Florida offshore acreage remained available for future leasing proposals rather than being statutorily off-limits.

for.name: Kathy Castor
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to ban new offshore drilling off Florida.

for.name: Francis Rooney
for.what_they_did: Original cosponsor supporting the offshore drilling ban.

for.name: 14 total cosponsors (11 of 231 House Democrats, 3 of 197 House Republicans)
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support of the ban on new Florida offshore leasing.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over offshore leasing
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or advanced the bill; it stalled at subcommittee referral.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsors split roughly 11 Democrats to 3 Republicans, all from Florida, reflecting bipartisan regional support rather than a party divide.

industries.note: The bill would have removed potential new drilling acreage off Florida from leasing, cutting off future expansion for the industry. The industry benefits from the bill's failure to advance.
Barring new drilling protects beaches and marine resources that drive Florida's coastal economy. The industry loses protection because the bill did not advance.
Avoiding new drilling reduces spill risk to Gulf and South Atlantic fisheries that support fishing livelihoods.
